rv.q: It’s an exhilarating rush of modern, mythic and tragic.
Veterans and novices alike will be enchanted.
I would challenge anyone not to have a good time with this.
Compression produces casualties. Some storylines feel undernourished and the dialogue struggles under the weight of exposition.
It’s baffling that in all that time no one noticed its deficiencies in plot and score.
Not a single one of the 27 belted-out songs has the power to resurrect it.
The whole evening was great fun and total fantasy – just go and lose yourself!

Death Note, first seen in Tokyo in 2015, comes swaggering into the capital for its English-language premiere (not counting a West End concert version three years ago) like some gleaming, glittering fantastical beast. This is a very big show in every sense: ambition, emotions, scale, spectacle, cast… and sheer entertainment value.
This is a dazzling piece of stagecraft, punchy in its score, a wonder in its design, a delight in its cast, and yet it is built on a saga simply too vast to survive the squeeze.
If there's one thing Death Note won't do this summer, it's leave you dying of boredom.
Akhila Krishnan’s flickering projections of neon lights and rain evocatively capture a sense of place, helping to pull together a stylish production that is dressed to kill.
It's a curiously distant experience, very much worthy of admiration, but falling well short of securing our love.
The lack of dramatic depth means Death Note never succeeds as a psychological drama, which the source material really is.
What makes this production such a resounding success is its commitment to not just do the best production of Death Note but to make a musical that stands up on its own two feet.
The stage grabs you before a single note plays.
This is a flawless adaptation that doesn’t require any knowledge of the manga or anime to engage with and enjoy.
It's a thrilling, surprisingly thoughtful musical that constantly asks where justice ends and the temptation to play God begins.
Death Note: The Musical has created something that feels both fresh and spectacular, and it deserves the chance to reach the wider audience it has clearly earned.
The cast and crew poured talent and effort into their brilliant performance and I wholeheartedly enjoyed the show.
Utilising the Barbican Theatre’s stage to its fullest extent, this is a musical that earns the hype.
Death Note the musical was a magical experience!
The storytelling, performances, music and production design come together to create an impressive piece of musical theatre, with plenty to appeal to those already familiar with the manga and anime.
Mass murder never looked (or sounded) so good!
What the musical lacks in philosophical rigour though it makes up for in production value.
Unfortunately, Death Note didn't convince us as a musical and perhaps should have stuck to its Post-Its rather than overreach for its musical notes.
The choreography – propulsive, passionate, and precision-tooled for greatness; the same can be said for the writing, acting, music and stagecraft – leaves you slack-jawed.

Its precision, scale and confident theatrical style make it feel unlike anything else currently playing in the West End, while the enthusiastic audience response demonstrates this cult phenomenon continues to resonate around the world.
There is lots to appreciate about this attempt to pack the essence of Death Note into a two-act musical, delivered at such visually ambitious, if not dizzying, scale.

cn.t: Critics praise Death Note's spectacular staging and propulsive energy, with strong performances from its cast, though some find the manga adaptation lacks psychological depth and works better for existing fans than newcomers.
